newsitem.title: EGYPT: Militant vows to attack Israel hit Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Militant vows to attack Israel hit Mideast peace.

text.p: Two militant Islamist groups vowed on Tuesday to carry out fresh suicide attacks inside Israel, deepening a crisis in the Middle East as a flurry of high-level meetings sought to revive a faltering peace process.

Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak said after talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Cairo that Israel should continue peace talks with Palestinians despite last week's suicide bombing in Jerusalem because peace was the only way to avoid further "terrorism".
The bombings last Wednesday, at a crowded Jerusalem market, left 15 dead including two bombers and jeopardised already shaky Middle East peace efforts.

Former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres, an architect of the historic 1993 interim peace deal with the PLO, warned his successor Benjamin Netanyahu that security crackdowns on Palestinians for the bombing risked handing victory to its perpetrators.

As diplomatic efforts to revive the peace process intensified ahead of a visit to the region by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, expected later this week, the military wing of the Islamic group Hamas promised a chain of attacks inside Israel.
"A chain of martyrdom attacks will come at the appropriate time to hit deep into Zionism," Hamas's Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades said in a statement faxed to Reuters in Jerusalem.

In Nabatiyeh, southern Lebanon, the fundamentalist Moslem Shi'ite group Hizbollah buried five of its guerrillas killed by Israeli commandos and also threatened to carry out suicide bombings inside Israel.

"Israel will witness explosions and suicide bombings inside all of its posts inside Palestine and inside occupied land," Hizbollah deputy secretary-general Naee'm Kassem told an angry crowd of several thousand at the fighters' funeral procession.

Mubarak, speaking a few hours after Israeli complaints that Yasser Arafat had yet to act against anti-Israeli militants believed to be behind the suicide bomb attack, warned of the danger of weakening the Palestinian leader's position.
He said Arafat was not "powerful enough" to implement the tough measures Israel demanded of him.

"I remember when Mr Rabin was in power, they may get offended when I say that, but this is a good example. When there was an explosion or terrorist action in Tel Aviv, right away after that he (Rabin) said 'I am going to continue negotiations for peace," Mubarak told reporters.

"It's a very wise statement because the only way to avoid terrorism and to avoid violence is to go through the peace process, because this terroristic action may be to hinder progress in the peace process," he added.

Levy told Israel Radio on his return home that Mubarak had denounced violence and "called on Arafat to fight terrorism because terrorism endangers everything, the entire region, and this is his (Arafat's) obligation.

"One should not scoff at or take lightly the fact that Egypt and its president are expressing themselves clearly and forcefully on the matter...namely that security cooperation, the war against terrorism and prevention of violence should be ensured," he added.

Arab League permanent representatives, meeting at the request of the Palestinians, condemned as a declaration of war Israel's crackdown in Palestinian self-rule areas after the suicide bombing, for which the League held Israel responsible.

"The League's council confirms that this explosive situation and the acts of violence in the region... are one result of stopping the peace process due to Israel's practices and not adhering to signed agreements," the League's statement said.

Peres said Netanyahu, who ousted him in knife-edge elections last year after a wave of similar attacks on Israelis, was weakening Palestinian authorities at the same time as he told them to take tough action against the militant Hamas movement.
"I think one has to be very careful not to allow Hamas to emerge as the winners of this action, particularly as they are the ones who did it," Peres told Reuters in an interview.
A leaflet issued in Hamas's name last week claimed responsibility for the suicide bomb attack, but Israeli and PLO officials questioned its authenticity.
Hamas, which regards the Israel-PLO interim peace deals as a sell-out of their goal to found an Islamic state in Palestine, has in the past launched waves of suicide attacks in Israel.
In a report sure to enrage Palestinians, the Israeli group Peace Now said settlers had plans to double the number of housing units for Jews in the occupied West Bank.

Settler leaders denied the report and a spokesman for Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, the cabinet member who authorises construction in Jewish settlements, said "the facts and figures are, to say the least, incorrect".
Jordan's King Hussein is to send his brother, Crown Prince Hassan, and Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali for talks with Netanyahu on Wednesday.
